issues.legal_issue: Capitalisation of net income may be used as the sole method for determining compensation for the acquisition of a public utility undertaking when it is a relevant method of valuing the undertaking as a whole.
material_facts: The acquired property was a public utility undertaking engaged in the manufacture and supply of gas.
The governing compensation method capitalised the undertaking’s average net income.
The challenge treated the income method as irrelevant because the undertaking had public-service obligations and included tangible assets.
issues.conclusion: Capitalisation of net income was a recognised and relevant method of valuing a public utility undertaking as an integrated whole; the possibility that another appropriate method might produce a higher value did not make this method invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) of the Constitution as it stood after the Fourth Amendment and before the Twenty-fifth Amendment, a specified compensation principle could be challenged if irrelevant to determining compensation, but not merely because another appropriate principle might produce a more generous result. The Court applied R. C. Cooper v. Union of India, which recognises capitalisation of net annual profit as a method of valuation and ordinarily treats an undertaking acquired as a unit as an integrated whole. The Court also relied on the principle that an undertaking’s profit-yielding capacity is a basic consideration in its value.

predicates.net_income_capitalization_used: The legislature uses the undertaking’s net income as the basis for determining its value.

issues.definition: When a compensation challenge concerns an acquired public utility taken as a unit and the valuation uses its net income, the method is treated as relevant.

issues.legal_issue: Using a multi-year period immediately before the transfer of management to calculate average net income is not arbitrary merely because profits varied or some years were lean.
material_facts: The compensation method used average net income over the five complete years preceding the year in which management and control were transferred.
The company argued that special circumstances had made profits particularly low during some years in that period.
The Court observed that using only the final year or averaging fewer preceding years could have produced lower compensation.
issues.conclusion: The choice of the five-year period immediately preceding the transfer of management and control was not arbitrary.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2), the selection of a relevant compensation principle is not invalid merely because another method could produce a different or more favourable result. The Court considered the period reasonably related to the value of the undertaking on or about acquisition and referred to Appleton Water Co. v. Railroad Commission in discussing the choice of a valuation period.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature’s selection of a capitalisation multiplier is not invalid merely because a higher multiplier could be derived from the return on gilt-edged securities.
material_facts: The compensation method capitalised average net income using a multiplier selected by the legislature.
The company argued that a higher multiplier should have been used because gilt-edged securities were yielding a higher return at the time of acquisition.
The Court considered that the appropriate return depended on circumstances including the nature of the property, the expected return on comparable investments, and capital-market conditions.
issues.conclusion: The Court would not substitute a higher multiplier for the one selected by the legislature merely because gilt-edged securities provided a different benchmark return.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as applicable to the acquisition, did not make the return on gilt-edged securities an invariable basis for selecting a multiplier. R. C. Cooper v. Union of India identifies capitalisation as a recognised valuation method, while the appropriate rate depends on relevant circumstances; choosing among appropriate principles or rates is for the legislature unless the specified basis is irrelevant.
